title: X: The Man with the X-Ray Eyes

facts.text: American International Pictures released this in fall 1963 as a double feature with Dementia 13, an early horror film directed by a young Francis Ford Coppola.
Star Ray Milland (Dr. James Xavier) won the 1945 Best Actor Oscar for The Lost Weekend, and was the first Welsh-born actor to win an Academy Award.
Harold J. Stone (Dr. Sam Brant) was a longtime friend of Jerry Lewis, who cast him in three of his films, including The Big Mouth (1967).
Director Roger Corman shot this in about three weeks on a budget of roughly $300,000, and later called its success a miracle.
Diana Van der Vlis (Dr. Diane Fairfax) kept a 20-inch pet alligator in her New York apartment for her two children.
Roger Corman's first draft made the hero a jazz musician on drugs. After four or five pages he threw it out and went back to his original idea: a scientist.
Principal photography began March 4, 1963, at Republic Studios in Studio City, California, according to the AFI Catalog.
Corman was famous for lean budgets, yet he hired Oscar-winning cinematographer Floyd Crosby, who shot many of his films.
Watch the coffee: Ray Milland (Dr. Xavier) pulls a second cup from the machine without paying or waiting for it to fill.
A July 1963 Variety review credited the film's visual trick as "Spectarama." The effects were done cheaply, with colored lighting and filmed construction sites.
Goof: Dr. Brant is told to put one drop in each of Dr. Xavier's eyes, but two drops land in the first eye.
Director Tim Burton developed a remake script with writer Bryan Goluboff, but it never got made.
Gold Key Comics published a comic book adaptation of the film in September 1963.
John Hoyt (Dr. Willard Benson) is one of the few actors to appear on both the original Star Trek and the original Battlestar Galactica.
Composer Les Baxter scored many Corman and American International pictures of the era, and his motifs were often interchangeable between films.
Director Roger Corman said star Ray Milland once named this film and The Lost Weekend as the two movies he was proudest of, per Corman's commentary as reported by MovieFanFare.
Richard Scheib of Moria called the party scene hilarious: the nudity is hidden below the waist or by turned backs.
Corman dropped his jazz-musician draft partly because drug-using characters of the era had to be punished for their 'lack of intelligence' under Hays Code-style rules, MovieFanFare reports.
The dancers at the party are doing The Twist, which was popular from late 1959 to 1963.
Look closely: when a woman facing away turns slightly, the edge of a cover-up on her chest shows.
Cinematographer Floyd Crosby, father of rock star David Crosby, used kaleidoscopic filters and colored gels in Pathécolor to suggest sight beyond the visible spectrum, says Inverse.
This was the final film of veteran character actor Morris Ankrum.
The close-ups of Dr. Xavier's hands during the heart operation are footage of a real surgeon's hands.
Goof: Dr. Xavier operates on the girl's heart but his hands never pick up any blood.
The film won the "Silver Spaceship" award at the first International Festival of Science Fiction Film in Trieste, Italy, in 1963.
The film's trippy vision effects reflect Corman's interest in psychedelic culture, which he pushed further in his 1967 film The Trip, according to Inverse's retrospective.
Rotten Tomatoes gives the film 88%. Its consensus calls it "one of Roger Corman's most effective movies."
The two hecklers Crane picks on are Dick Miller and Jonathan Haze, who became Corman cult icons through A Bucket of Blood and The Little Shop of Horrors.
On The Tonight Show in 1972, Ray Milland said this film was terrible but that Don Rickles (Crane) had been brilliant in it.
Critic Paul Willemen wrote in 1970 that Xavier's growing personal isolation is paralleled by his geographic isolation, with the pursuing helicopter standing in for a vengeful god.
Richard Scheib of Moria reads the film through the Icarus myth, calling Ray Russell's script "remarkably tortured and personalised."
The New York Times praised the originality of the screenplay and Ray Milland's performance as Dr. James Xavier, according to the AFI Catalog.
In Britain in 1964 it played on a double bill with Corman's The Masque of the Red Death, and later aired on TV simply as "X."
The film originally had a five-minute prologue about the human senses. It was cut from later prints, bringing the runtime down to 79 minutes.
Several of the extras waiting in the clinic also played townspeople in Mayberry on The Andy Griffith Show.
Writer Tim Lucas notes the film opened billed as shot in a new 'Spectarama' process, and argues it was more a marketing hook for audiences than a true photographic advance.
Bauhaus (on 1981's Mask) and Blue Öyster Cult (on 1998's Heaven Forbid) each have a song that references this film.
When the film opened in Omaha in October 1963, horror star Peter Lorre visited the city to promote it, according to the AFI Catalog.
The film's X-ray perspective shots used Spectarama, a photographic technique credited to its inventor, John C. Howard, according to a review at Realweegiemidget Reviews.
The closing montage with the credits appears to have influenced Martin Scorsese's treatment of the end of Taxi Driver.
The skeletal skyscraper was real: Corman filmed the Department of Water & Power building in downtown Los Angeles while it was still under construction.
Corman never stayed in one place: he often shot a second film at the same location to spread the costs.
Corman has said Ray Milland was very enthusiastic after reading the script and was proud of the finished film, according to the Maniacs and Monsters review.
Goof: the dealer shows a king, flips a face card and announces "eighteen." Two face cards make twenty.
Don Rickles (Crane) later voiced Mr. Potato Head in the first three Toy Story films.
Rumor says the film once ended with 'I can still see!' Corman said it wasn't scripted: he shot the line on a whim, disliked it and scrapped it, per a Million Monkey Theater review.
Goof: a helicopter announces "This is the California Highway Patrol," but the California line is about 50 miles from Las Vegas.
Corman saved a dollar: Dr. Xavier starts in a Lincoln Continental with whitewalls, but the wreck is a junker painted blue with blackwalls and no hubcaps.
The chase was filmed on Soledad Canyon Road in California, where almost all of Steven Spielberg's Duel (1971) was shot.
The unfinished highway was a stretch of what became Interstate 15, then U.S. 91. The distance sign was shot near today's Primm, Nevada.
Richard Scheib of Moria called the revival-tent climax "wonderfully overwrought" and praised the film's grand vision despite the thrift.
Stephen King, in Danse Macabre, called this "one of the most interesting and offbeat little horror movies ever made" and ranked the ending among film's most shuddery gross-out scenes.
American International Pictures released the film September 18, 1963 at 79 minutes, according to Wikipedia. In France it drew 53,087 admissions.
Stephen King wrote of a rumored longer ending where Xavier cries "I can still see!" Corman denied it was shot, but said King's version was better than his own.
